text: Minus twenty-five degrees. Wind like broken glass. You're wearing a hoodie and sneakers.
Ten minutes ago you were in a museum in twenty twenty-six.
No phone signal. No buildings. No people. Just snow, all the way to the edge of the world.
Hello? Is anyone there? Hello?!
Something answers. It's four metres tall. It's covered in hair. And it's looking right at you.
What if you woke up thirty thousand years ago?
Your job is simple. Mop the Ice Age hall. Don't touch anything.
Two more hours. Just two more hours.
There's one case you always walk past.|A carved bone, thirty thousand years old.|Covered in tiny scratches nobody can explain.
The sign says the scratches might be the oldest calendar ever found.|Days, counted by somebody, one line at a time.
Tonight, the scratches are glowing.
Okay. That's not normal.
You touch the glass. And the museum disappears.
The cold is the first thing that tries to kill you.
At minus twenty-five with strong wind, bare skin can get frostbite in under thirty minutes.|Your body pulls blood away from your fingers to save your heart.
No signal. Twelve percent. Of course.
Okay. Think. Don't panic. What did that survival guy say? Get out of the wind.
You do the one smart thing you remember from a survival video. You dig.
Snow is full of trapped air.|Inside a small snow cave, your body heat can keep the air near zero, even when it's minus thirty outside.
You survive the first night. Barely.
In the morning, you finally see where you are. And it's beautiful. And terrifying.
Thirty thousand years ago, ice sheets up to three kilometres thick covered the north of Europe.|The sea was so low, you could walk from France to Britain.
There are no roads. No towns. No people. Just animals that don't exist anymore.
A woolly mammoth could weigh six tonnes. And cave lions were even bigger than the lions alive today.
And somewhere out there, something is following your footprints.
The whole planet was about six degrees colder on average than today.|That sounds small.|It's the difference between our world and a frozen one.
Okay. Okay. I'm in the Ice Age. I'm actually in the Ice Age.
Day two. You inventory your survival kit. A phone. A pen. A frozen water bottle. One granola bar.
Rubbing sticks. Like in the movies. How hard can it be?
Very hard. Forty minutes later, you have blisters. And no fire.
Then you notice the stones in the riverbank. Some are grey and sharp. Some are shiny, like gold.
Strike flint against a mineral called pyrite, and you get real sparks.|Scientists think Neanderthals were already making fire this way fifty thousand years ago.
Yes! Yes! Fire! I made fire!
For the first time in two days, you can feel your fingers.|You eat half the granola bar.|You save the other half.
And in the dark, someone sees it.
Day three. You wake up surrounded.
Hrah! Tuun ka!
They're human. Just like you. Same brain. Same body. Thirty thousand years of history between you.
Languages change so fast that English from a thousand years ago is almost impossible to read today.|From thirty thousand years ago, you'd share not a single word.
I'm... friendly? Friend. I'm a friend.
The little one breaks the silence. He points at your fire. Then at you. And he laughs.
Fa-ra! Fa-ra!
Tuun? Fa-ra... Eli?
Fara. Fire. Your first word. And the reason they don't kill you.
They take you back to their camp. Twenty people. Mammoth bones holding up the tents.
Scientists estimate that only a few thousand people lived in all of Western Europe back then.|Fewer than in one small town today.
Everyone works.|Everyone is useful.|And you?|You can't sew.|You can't hunt.|You can't even skin a rabbit.
Hmm. Kiti-ka.
The old woman says one word. You learn later what it means. Little baby.
Then Pip finds your pen.|He draws a horse on your notebook.|And the whole band gathers around, amazed that ink comes out of a stick.
But you have one thing they don't. You know how the story ends.
Day nine. Pip has a fever. Then his mother. Then three more.
And you realise something horrible. You brought this.
When Europeans reached the Americas in fourteen ninety-two, they carried diseases nobody there had ever met.|In some places, up to nine out of ten people died.
It's me. It's my cold. They've never had it.
You can't make medicine.|But you know three things that save more lives than any pill.|Keep the sick apart.|Boil the water.|Wash your hands.
Water. Fire. Boil. Hands. Like this. Everyone, like this!
Eli... Pip?
It takes eleven days. Everyone lives. And Tor never looks at you the same way again.
Day thirty. Winter is coming. Real winter. The band needs meat. A lot of it.
So you give them something from the future. Just a stick with a hook on the end.
A spear-thrower works like an extra arm.|It can launch a spear at over a hundred and fifty kilometres an hour.|The oldest ones we've found are around twenty thousand years old.
Ha! Eli! Again! Again!
The next morning, the hunters go after the biggest animal in the valley.
And everything goes wrong. The mammoth turns. Nia slips on the ice.
Nia! Move!
Your throw isn't perfect. But it's close enough to scare a six-tonne animal away.
That night, Nia carves a little picture on the bone she wears around her neck.|A stick figure with a hood.
Day sixty. A storm hits so hard you can't see your own hand.
When it's over, Tor is missing.
Tor! Tor! Can you hear me?
You find him at the bottom of a gully. His leg is broken. Night is coming.
Nia, help me! We tie his leg straight. Like this. Then we pull.
Archaeologists have found skeletons from the Ice Age with healed broken bones.|Somebody fed them, carried them, and kept them alive for months.|People were caring for each other long before medicine.
Eli... ana-ka. Ana-ka.
Ana-ka. Brother. That's what he calls you now.
You carve another line on your bone.|Sixty lines.|One for every day.|Just like the bone in the museum.
Day one hundred. The band takes you somewhere special. A cave deep in the mountain.
Real cave paintings in France are more than thirty thousand years old.|Lions, horses, rhinos, painted so well they look like they're moving in the torchlight.
Your phone has one percent left. You record one last message.
If anyone ever finds this... I'm okay. I have a family here now.
Then you take the charcoal. And you paint something no one here has ever seen.
The screen goes black. Forever.
Eli. Friend. Always.
Twenty twenty-six. A cave in southern France.
Lights on panel seven, please. Thank you.
Doctor Lena Voss has studied this cave for twenty years. She knows every painting in it.
That... wasn't there yesterday. That's a person in a hood. Holding... a screen?
Her team runs every test they have. The pigment. The charcoal. The dust on top of it.
The charcoal is thirty thousand years old. And next to the figure, someone scratched four letters.
E. L. I. And a smiley face.
What's the one thing you would take with you thirty thousand years into the past?|Tell us in the comments.|And subscribe, so you don't miss part two.
